# Movable-frame beehive (`beekeeping_movable_frame`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/agriculture.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Agriculture & food (`agriculture`)
- Core idea: Bees keep open a passage of 6–9 mm (the 'bee space'): narrower gaps they glue shut, wider ones they fill with comb. Hang rectangular wooden frames in a box so that this working passage remains between the finished comb faces and between comb and box, and every comb can be lifted out, inspected and put back; honey is taken from an upper box and the colony lives on, instead of being killed with sulphur as in straw skeps. The simplest version is a trough covered by wooden bars 32–35 mm wide laid edge to edge, with sloping sides so the combs are not fixed to the walls. Smoke calms the bees.
- Pitfalls:
  - Wrong spacing: frames get glued solid or bridged with wild comb and cannot be moved
  - Taking too much honey in autumn; a colony needs 15–20 kg to survive a northern winter
  - Calling the large bee the 'king'; she is a female, the mother of the hive
  - Moving combs between sick and healthy hives, which spreads foulbrood
  - Giving honey to infants under one year (botulism risk)
- History: egypt: c. 2400 BC – horizontal clay hives in the sun temple of Nyuserre; c. 900 BC a large apiary at Tel Rehov in the Levant; greece: 1682 – George Wheler publishes his account of Greek basket hives with movable top bars; continuity from antiquity is uncertain; china: by c. 2nd c. AD – the eastern honey bee kept in log and wall hives; americas: pre-Columbian – Maya keep stingless bees in log hives; 1622 European honey bee brought to Virginia; 1851 L. L. Langstroth applies the bee space (patent 1852); europe: 1609 Butler shows the 'king' is a queen; 1789–92 Huber's leaf hive; 1838 Dzierzon's movable bars; 1865 Hruschka's honey extractor

  - L. L. Langstroth, Langstroth on the Hive and the Honey-Bee: A Bee Keeper's Manual (1853)
